nameStory: Worm Weed gets its descriptive name from its long, twisted, worm-like appearance as it grows in tangled masses along the shoreline. The scientific name 'contorta' means 'twisted' in Latin, reinforcing this snake-like characteristic that makes it so recognizable among seaweeds.
description: Worm Weed is a small marine algae that you'll find growing as an epiphyte, meaning it attaches itself to other seaweeds and marine plants rather than directly to rocks. This reddish-brown seaweed forms long, narrow, tube-like fronds that twist and curl in characteristic worm-like shapes. It's relatively small compared to the larger kelps and rockweeds, creating delicate tangles along New England's rocky shores.

idTips.label: Twisted tube shape
idTips.description: Long, narrow, hollow tubes that twist and contort like earthworms, feeling soft and squishy when fresh from the water

idTips.label: Epiphytic growth
idTips.description: Always found growing attached to other seaweeds or marine plants, never directly on bare rocks like many other algae

idTips.label: Reddish-brown color
idTips.description: Deep brownish-red to purplish-red coloration that becomes more vibrant when wet and darker when dried

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Much smaller and more delicate than the robust rockweeds and kelps around it, forming modest tangles rather than large masses

idTips.label: Soft texture
idTips.description: Feels gelatinous and slippery when wet, lacking the firm or leathery texture of larger brown seaweeds

habitat: Look for Worm Weed in the intertidal zone along New England's rocky coastlines, particularly in tide pools and areas that stay moist between tides. It grows as an epiphyte on other seaweeds like rockweed and sea lettuce, preferring protected coves and areas with good water circulation rather than exposed, wave-battered shores.

seasonality.spring: Fresh growth begins appearing on host seaweeds, with bright reddish-brown coloration and soft, pliable texture from spring tides and cooler water temperatures.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with the most abundant and vibrant specimens visible during low tides, though hot sunny days may cause temporary bleaching of exposed individuals.
seasonality.fall: Still readily observable but may appear darker and more weathered from summer exposure, with some fronds beginning to break down in rough fall weather.
seasonality.winter: Often persists through winter storms but may be reduced in abundance, with remaining specimens appearing darker and more brittle from cold and wave action.

funFact: Worm Weed is essentially a seaweed hitchhiker—it spends its entire life growing on other seaweeds rather than claiming its own patch of rock real estate, making it one of nature's most committed freeloaders!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with young kelp fronds or other small red algae, but its distinctive twisted, worm-like tubes and epiphytic lifestyle (always growing on other seaweeds) set it apart. Remember: if it looks like twisted rubber tubing growing on another seaweed, you've found Worm Weed.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name suggesting it might be a flowering plant or terrestrial weed, Worm Weed is actually a marine algae with no relation to land-based weeds—the name simply refers to its worm-like appearance and its tendency to form tangled masses that early naturalists considered weedy.
compareHints: As the only Dumontia species commonly found in New England waters, Worm Weed is most easily compared to other small red algae in its family. Unlike its relatives, it maintains the distinctive twisted, tube-like form and consistent epiphytic growth habit, making it relatively easy to distinguish once you know what to look for.
